Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.23571.question: What are BMuon's measured post-training channel-pruning results and language-model results versus Muon and other baselines at matched training compute or model quality? What experiments control for accuracy before pruning?

passages.text: Modern Transformer models incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference time, motivating compression for more efficient deployment ( Kwon et al., 2022 ) . Pruning is a natural approach to this problem, but practical gains depend on the sparsity structure: unstructured sparsity often requires specialized kernels or hardware, whereas structured pruning removes entire computational units and translates directly into efficiency gains ( Wen et al., 2016 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Feed-forward modules can account for roughly two thirds of Transformer parameters ( Geva et al., 2021 ) , making their hidden channels a natural target for structured compression. Global pruning ranks channels across layers jointly, allowing different layers to retain different numbers of channels ( Lee et al., 2021 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Post-pruning fine-tuning adds computational cost, especially for large models ( Kwon et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , motivating compressibility to emerge during training so that pruning requires little or no recovery. Figure 1 : Post-training global MLP pruning on ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16. Mean ± \pm std over 3 seeds. See Appendix E.1 .

Muon has demonstrated strong training efficiency across model scales, from small vision and language-model benchmarks to billion-parameter language models ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) . Its matrix update can be viewed as a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball, giving Muon a steepest-descent interpretation in spectral-norm geometry ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) . Prior work has shown that implicit bias can depend on optimization geometry ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . For Muon, recent theory identifies a spectral-norm margin bias in linear and smooth homogeneous models ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) . Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers degrade rapidly under structured MLP pruning, suggesting that Muon’s spectral geometry does not by itself encourage structured compressibility. As shown in Figure 1 , a Muon-trained ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K collapses after only 30 % 30\% global MLP channel pruning, with Top-1 accuracy falling from 75.23 % 75.23\% to 3.17 % 3.17\% . In contrast, our proposed Budget Muon (BMuon) algorithm retains 74.08 % 74.08\% Top-1 accuracy after 70 % 70\% pruning, nearly matching its 74.17 % 74.17\% accuracy before pruning, with no post-pruning recovery. This raises the central question: can Muon’s spectral geometry be modified to encourage structured compressibility?

To address this question, we introduce BMuon, which reweights Muon’s spectral geometry under a single global budget K K shared across all hidden channels of all MLP blocks. For hidden channel j j in block ℓ \ell , BMuon assigns an allocation μ j ℓ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mu_{j}^{\ell}\in[0,1] to the corresponding row of the up-projection matrix and column of the down-projection matrix, with ∑ ℓ , j μ j ℓ = K \sum_{\ell,j}\mu_{j}^{\ell}=K . For a fixed allocation, BMuon introduces a diagonal reweighting inside Muon’s spectral-norm constraint, with the components of the update variable corresponding to channel j j in block ℓ \ell weighted according to its allocation μ j ℓ \mu_{j}^{\ell} . BMuon chooses the allocation globally, intuitively asking where the update budget should be spent to obtain the greatest first-order decrease in the loss.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

inspect:2610.19844.question: In LLM pretraining experiments, how does residual-correction subspace optimization compare with GaLore, FRUGAL, full-space Muon, and AdamW on validation loss or perplexity, peak GPU memory, optimizer-state memory, and full-step throughput at matched model size and token budget?

passages.text: Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

In this section, we provide the omitted details of the LLM supervised finetuning (SFT) experiments. For the instruction-following task, we train on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU and adopt a device micro-batch size of 16 16 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for Muon, GaLore, GoLore, GUM, and PMRC, and a device micro-batch size of 8 8 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is 128 128 in both cases. For the mathematical reasoning task, we train on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs and adopt a device micro-batch size of 4 4 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for the same methods and a device micro-batch size of 2 2 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is again 128 128 . For AdamW-based methods, we use the standard coefficients β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 and β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 . For Muon-based methods, the momentum coefficient is set to 1 − β = 0.95 1-\beta=0.95 with Nesterov momentum enabled. The matrix sign is approximated using 5 5 Newton–Schulz iterations, while one-dimensional parameters and embedding layers are optimized with AdamW.

Hyperparameter Tuning. For each model and optimization method we select the learning rate by a grid search over { 1 × 10 − 5 , 2 × 10 − 5 , 4 × 10 − 5 , 8 × 10 − 5 } \{1\times 10^{-5},2\times 10^{-5},4\times 10^{-5},8\times 10^{-5}\} for the instruction-following task and { 8 × 10 − 6 , 1 × 10 − 5 , 3 × 10 − 5 , 5 × 10 − 5 , 7 × 10 − 5 } \{8\times 10^{-6},1\times 10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5},7\times 10^{-5}\} for the mathematical-reasoning task. PMRC uses a residual cap at a ratio of 4 4 and we grid search γ ∈ { 2000 , 4000 , 8000 , 16000 } \gamma\in\{2000,4000,8000,16000\} . We select the parameters that achieve the highest accuracy on benchmarks. Additional results. We present the prompt-level and instruction-level strict accuracy on the IFEval benchmark in Table 9 . For completeness, we include the results of GUM with rank r = 256 r=256 , in addition to the memory-matched setting with r = 128 r=128 used in the main experiments. PMRC outperforms GUM at both ranks on all three models in both metrics. We also report the peak allocated GPU memory of all methods in Table 10 , measured on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU with torch.compile disabled. PMRC requires the lowest peak memory across all models. Table 10: Peak allocated GPU memory (GiB) during full-parameter SFT. We use a micro-batch size of 16 16 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for IFEval and a micro-batch size of 4 4 with 32 32 gradient accumulation steps for GSM8K. All memory measurements are performed on a single H20 GPU.

For all ablations, we pretrain LLaMA-150M on the C4 dataset for 9900 9900 steps with a sequence length of 512 512 and a global batch size of 512 512 . We refresh the projection basis every 100 100 steps and, unless otherwise stated, set the residual cap to ρ = 4 \rho=4 . Effect of the subspace rank. We vary the projection rank over r ∈ { 64,128,256,512 } r\in\{64,128,256,512\} with the residual weight fixed at γ = 8192 \gamma=8192 and all other settings unchanged. Increasing r r expands the subspace in which momentum is maintained and the matrix-sign transformation is applied. As shown in Figure 3 , a larger rank reduces the validation loss, but also increases the memory required to store the projection basis and the projected momentum. For a parameter matrix of size m × n m\times n , this memory cost scales as O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . These results illustrate the trade-off between validation performance and optimizer-state memory when choosing the subspace rank. Effect of the residual weight. We fix the rank at r = 256 r=256 and vary the residual weight over γ ∈ { 0 , 1024 , 2048 , 4096 , 8192 } \gamma\in\{0,1024,2048,4096,8192\} with all other settings unchanged. Since the residual cap remains active, γ \gamma serves as an upper bound on the effective weight applied to each parameter matrix rather than its exact value. As shown in Figure 4 , the validation loss decreases monotonically as γ \gamma increases over the tested range, with diminishing improvements at larger values. In particular, γ = 0 \gamma=0 removes the residual correction and yields the highest validation loss. This comparison supports the benefit of incorporating gradient information from the orthogonal complement in LLM pretraining. Figure 5: Effect of the residual cap on PMRC.

passages.text: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

We thus introduce Ori , a streaming k k -PCA-based O ja-style updated low- r ank i terative optimizer, designed to exploit the slow-drift regime of LLM gradient subspaces. Rather than treating each subspace estimation as an independent, “cold-start” problem—as is the case with periodic SVD recomputation in GaLore—Ori treats subspace estimation as a continuous tracking problem. The core innovation of Ori lies in its drift-aware bootstrapping mechanism: we carry over (transfer) the subspace basis from previous steps as the initialization state for the current step. Because of the slow-drift phenomenon, the prior basis provides a suitable starting point that requires only a few lightweight, streaming k k -PCA-inspired updates to realign with the instantaneous gradient geometry. In practice, Ori instantiates this via the Oja++ algorithm [ 24 , 1 ] , which enables high-frequency basis rotations at a per-step cost of only 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ k 2 ) \mathcal{O}(dk^{2}) . This approach allows for a warm-start transfer of Adam-style first and second moments between successive bases, ensuring stable optimization dynamics. Beyond computational efficiency, we show that this formulation allows Ori to achieve provable sublinear dynamic regret bounds under drift, providing new theoretical tools and guarantees for tracking fidelity that static recomputation methods lack.

Empirically, Ori narrowly tracks the evolving gradient subspace and converts this tracking fidelity into end-to-end wins where it matters most: very low ranks. Under tight rank budgets, each dimension in the projector is precious, and stale misalignment is especially costly. Empirical results show that Ori reduces the performance gap of state-of-the-art low-rank baselines to the full-rank Adam optimizer by up to 69.3% on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task, where the optimizer state rank is 128 in contrast to the model embedding dimension of 2048. And on Roberta-Base fine-tuning tasks, where the ranks are even lower (8 or 4), Ori achieves superior performance on 10 out of 16 scenarios. Moreover, Ori achieved this superior performance with one of the lowest computation budgets. See Figure 1 for a performance–memory overview on LLaMA-1B pre-training, where Ori consistently sits on the bottom-left frontier. Through ablation, we observe that (i) increasing the projector-update period degrades performance—quantifying the cost of staleness, and (ii) injecting a small carry-over (via a drift coefficient ρ ≈ 0.99 \rho\approx 0.99 ) improves accuracy—confirming the value of continuity and statistic transfer. Across pre-training and fine-tuning settings, Ori consistently improves the performance–memory trade-off over LoRA, GaLore, and OSD in the low-rank regime, thereby reducing the gap to full-rank Adam. Our primary contributions in this work are as follows: • We identify and quantify slow gradient subspace drift during LLM training and argue that exploiting its continuity – not merely reacting to it – matters for low-rank optimization.

• We propose Ori, a drift-aware low-rank optimizer that equips gap-free streaming k k -PCA with moment transfer to achieve continuous, high-frequency projector updates at negligible cost. • We provide theoretical support via new dynamic-regret bounds under drift, yielding sublinear regret in the noiseless setting with mild dependence on the consecutive drift parameter. • We present empirical results showing Ori’s superior performance under stringent rank constraints, with ablations isolating the roles of update frequency and drift-aware continuity.

We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

Our answer starts with a simple observation: once the backbone is frozen, the loss does not observe an adapted matrix T T directly, but only through a finite-rank linear map determined by the frozen activations. Concretely, if H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}] is the matrix of frozen input features across the N N training samples, the empirical loss depends on T T only through the product T ​ H TH . We call rank ⁡ ( Φ ) \rank(\Phi) , where Φ ⁡ ( T ) = T ​ H \Phi(T)=TH , the bottleneck rank of the adapted block. The same principle applies blockwise to multiple adapted stages and attention heads. Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output. This yields exact low-rank existence results without linearizing the network around the pretrained weights. For multi-head attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , the same principle becomes sharper because attention introduces additional invariances: row-wise softmax is unchanged by additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and the frozen output projection. Table 1: Comparison with the closest related theoretical analyses of LoRA. This work Jang et al. (2024) Kim et al. (2025) Requires NTK linearization No Yes No Multilayer multi-head attention bound Yes (Thm. 4.4 ) No No Spurious local minima excluded No (Prop. 4.9 ) Yes (NTK) Partial Additional loss assumptions Differentiability and stagewise C 1 C^{1} regularity NTK-regime conditions Restricted strong convexity and smoothness Generalization bounds Yes Yes No Our contribution is summarized as follows.

• Low-rank representer theorem for trace-norm fine-tuning. For a frozen network in which an adapted block T T is observed only through a finite-rank linear map Φ ⁡ ( T ) \Phi(T) of bottleneck rank d Φ d_{\Phi} , we prove that the trace-norm-regularized problem has a global minimizer whose rank is controlled by d Φ d_{\Phi} ; see Theorem 4.1 . The multi-stage extension is Theorem 4.3 . • Rank bounds from attention invariances. For multi-head attention, query and key updates are observable only through centered score subspaces because row-wise softmax is invariant to row-wise additive constants. Value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. Combining these invariances with projector compression gives the optimizer-dependent subspace rank bounds in Theorem 4.4 . • Generic first-order rank deficiency for factorized LoRA. For the weight-decayed LoRA factorization, we prove that after a generic positive semidefinite perturbation, full-column-rank first-order stationary points are excluded whenever the Pataki–Barvinok rank threshold exceeds the dimension of the associated family of symmetric KKT matrices; see Theorem 4.7 . The multistage and attention consequence are Theorem C.9 and Corollary 4.8 . This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation. • Perturbation transfer and generalization. We show that global minimizers of the perturbed factorized objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm-regularized problem when the perturbation is small; see Theorem 4.10 .

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA .

This raises a question: how much gradient information lies outside the current tangent space? We analyze the tangent-space residual gradient across ten representative LoRA variants ( Fig. 1 ) and identify two consistent properties. First, the residual accounts for more than 85% of the total gradient energy across all methods. Second, it exhibits strong spectral concentration: the leading singular component captures more than 87% of the residual energy, while the top four capture more than 94%. These findings reveal that the current tangent space leaves substantial gradient information unexploited, yet most of this information can be recovered through a very low-rank approximation. A natural idea to exploit the residual gradient is to continually incorporate its principal directions into the trainable subspace. However, increasing the rank incurs a proportional parameter cost, whereas replacing existing factors at a fixed rank can discard accumulated adaptation information and disrupt training continuity. ReLoRA [ 20 ] , Flora [ 8 ] , and GaLore [ 47 ] also switch low-rank subspaces during training, primarily to overcome rank limitations or reduce training memory, but do not explicitly target gradient components outside the current tangent space. The key challenge is therefore to incorporate these principal residual directions within a fixed rank budget while retaining learned information, maintaining training stability, and preserving mergeability into the pre-trained weights.

To address this challenge, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch that accumulates task-specific directions as in standard LoRA and a dynamic branch that periodically absorbs principal residual directions outside the current tangent space. We prove that, under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints, the optimal update for a local quadratic model is given by the truncated SVD of the tangent-space residual gradient. Crucially, this residual inherits a factored structure from backpropagation, enabling its products with narrow matrices to be computed directly from cached input activations and output gradients. This structure allows us to construct matrix-free operators for Matrix-Free Randomized SVD, which extracts the principal residual directions via randomized SVD [ 7 ] without explicitly forming the residual gradient. To incorporate these directions while maintaining training stability, we introduce Controlled Write-back mechanism, which merges them with the current dynamic branch update, compresses the result back to the original rank, and bounds the relative change at each refresh. After training, both branches are merged into the pre-trained weights, yielding the same inference cost as standard LoRA.

We evaluate DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks: the 19 image classification tasks in VTAB-1K; object detection and instance segmentation on MS COCO; open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation (OVDG-SS) in both real-to-real and synthetic-to-real settings; eight commonsense reasoning tasks using LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B; and GLUE using DeBERTaV3-base. Under matched trainable parameter budgets, DT-LoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and its variants. On MS COCO, DT-LoRA at r = 16 r=16 achieves an average score of 46.6, exceeding LoRA at the same rank by 8.2 points and outperforming LieRA [ 29 ] , which uses twice as many trainable parameters. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA establishes new state-of-the-art results, surpassing the task-specific S 2 -Corr [ 46 ] despite being a general-purpose fine-tuning method. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify a geometric limitation of factorized LoRA: substantial gradient energy lies outside the current tangent space. Across ten representative LoRA variants, we show that this tangent-space residual exhibits strong spectral concentration, and establish that its truncated SVD yields the optimal update under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints for a local quadratic model. • We propose DT-LoRA, which partitions a fixed rank budget into Stable and Dynamic branches to incorporate principal residual directions. Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts these directions without materializing the residual gradient, while Controlled Write-back integrates them with accumulated updates and bounds the change at each refresh, enabling dynamic tangent-space adaptation without additional trainable parameters or inference overhead.

• We demonstrate the effectiveness of DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks, with consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants under matched trainable parameter budgets. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific methods and establishes new state-of-the-art results.

matches.abstract_excerpt: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA .

To this end, we train a LoRA model with rank r = 16 r=16 for diagnosis and decompose each learned update Δ ​ 𝑾 \Delta{\bm{W}} using singular value decomposition (SVD). Without retraining, we evaluate rank- k k approximations formed by retaining the top k k singular components. As shown in Figure 1 , we find that k = 3 k=3 yields the best downstream performance, whereas retaining additional components degrades it. This suggests that the full learned update is less effective than a lower-rank approximation of itself. A larger rank budget does not necessarily produce a more useful task-specific update. Figure 1: Effect of retained rank on accuracy. Model performance does not improve monotonically with increasing retained rank.

Motivated by this observation, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation ( ReGRA ), which helps the learned LoRA update make more effective use of its available rank. ReGRA first trains a standard LoRA adapter and then estimates task gradients with a small subset of the training data. To exhaust the allocated rank, we initialize a second-stage adapter with task gradients projected onto the two-sided complement of the first-stage update. With this first-stage estimation, we are able to leave the previously learned components unchanged, yet continually fulfil the update within the allocated rank. During second-stage training, we apply orthogonal regularization to maintain decorrelation between the two stages. After training, both updates can be merged into the base model, introducing no additional inference cost. We evaluate ReGRA using standard LoRA evaluation following ( Hu et al., 2023 ) and expand it to natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Under the same total-rank budget, ReGRA consistently achieves stronger overall performance across the evaluated benchmarks and even reaches the performance of the double-rank model. Ablation studies and further analysis support the effectiveness of residual-gradient initialization and update decorrelation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We reveal that standard LoRA training does not always make effective use of its allocated rank. We approach this problem from a task-gradient perspective, targeting directions not captured by the initial update.

• We propose ReGRA to exhaust the allocated rank. ReGRA is a two-stage adaptation method that estimates task gradients after standard LoRA training, projects out the components captured by the first-stage update, and uses the residual gradients to initialize a second-stage adapter. An orthogonal regularization maintains the decorrelation between the two updates. • We evaluate ReGRA on diverse benchmark sets, showing that it outperforms representative baselines and, in some settings, matches the performance of a model with twice the rank. Ablation studies support the efficacy and rationale of our design.

Low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) represents task-specific weight updates using two trainable low-rank factors, reducing the number of trainable parameters while retaining mergeability at inference ( Hu et al., 2021 ) . Subsequent variants improve its memory and parameter efficiency through quantization, factor freezing, or shared random projections ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ; Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) . Other methods explore adaptive rank allocation and rank-dependent scaling ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Valipour et al., 2023 ; Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) . Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA .

To this end, we train a LoRA model with rank r = 16 r=16 for diagnosis and decompose each learned update Δ ​ 𝑾 \Delta{\bm{W}} using singular value decomposition (SVD). Without retraining, we evaluate rank- k k approximations formed by retaining the top k k singular components. As shown in Figure 1 , we find that k = 3 k=3 yields the best downstream performance, whereas retaining additional components degrades it. This suggests that the full learned update is less effective than a lower-rank approximation of itself. A larger rank budget does not necessarily produce a more useful task-specific update. Figure 1: Effect of retained rank on accuracy. Model performance does not improve monotonically with increasing retained rank.

Motivated by this observation, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation ( ReGRA ), which helps the learned LoRA update make more effective use of its available rank. ReGRA first trains a standard LoRA adapter and then estimates task gradients with a small subset of the training data. To exhaust the allocated rank, we initialize a second-stage adapter with task gradients projected onto the two-sided complement of the first-stage update. With this first-stage estimation, we are able to leave the previously learned components unchanged, yet continually fulfil the update within the allocated rank. During second-stage training, we apply orthogonal regularization to maintain decorrelation between the two stages. After training, both updates can be merged into the base model, introducing no additional inference cost. We evaluate ReGRA using standard LoRA evaluation following ( Hu et al., 2023 ) and expand it to natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Under the same total-rank budget, ReGRA consistently achieves stronger overall performance across the evaluated benchmarks and even reaches the performance of the double-rank model. Ablation studies and further analysis support the effectiveness of residual-gradient initialization and update decorrelation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We reveal that standard LoRA training does not always make effective use of its allocated rank. We approach this problem from a task-gradient perspective, targeting directions not captured by the initial update.

• We propose ReGRA to exhaust the allocated rank. ReGRA is a two-stage adaptation method that estimates task gradients after standard LoRA training, projects out the components captured by the first-stage update, and uses the residual gradients to initialize a second-stage adapter. An orthogonal regularization maintains the decorrelation between the two updates. • We evaluate ReGRA on diverse benchmark sets, showing that it outperforms representative baselines and, in some settings, matches the performance of a model with twice the rank. Ablation studies support the efficacy and rationale of our design.

We study it in the exponential Hopfield model: one softmax attention step with the unlabelled examples as keys. A signal-to-noise analysis gives the overlap with an unseen archetype in closed form: a majority-rule law in which an attention entropy replaces the dataset entropy. At high temperature the archetype is lost in the crosstalk; at low temperature the softmax freezes on the closest training example, as in a random energy model, and the layer memorizes. In between, in a window widening with the square root of the network size, the layer pools the examples of the correct class and retrieves the unseen archetype as well as their majority vote allows, at any fixed load. matches.title: Noisy-Label Calibration with Multiple Unreliable Labels
matches.abstract_excerpt: In medical annotation and crowdsourcing, multiple annotators assign labels to each example, but these labels may be incorrect. matches.title: From Parallel to Sequential: Small-Batch Noise Restores Simplicity Bias of Muon
matches.abstract_excerpt: Simplicity bias, which can arise from sequential feature learning during training, has been proposed as a general explanation for the success of deep learning. passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

The 30 query cases include overlapping targets and a manually assembled distribution; the first ten items in each tier are not a random sample of all scientific literature. Benchmark authoring used an LLM, browser build identifiers were unavailable, history contamination cannot be excluded retrospectively, and one baseline credit follows an explicit historical convention. These factors limit causal and statistical interpretation. Future evaluation should freeze inputs, use isolated sessions, report first-attempt and recovered performance separately, and obtain independent relevance judgments for every returned work.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. These findings motivate focused scholarly retrieval with inspectable evidence; they do not establish general Deep Research superiority, calibrated novelty assessment, or a matched baseline cost advantage.

passages.text: Recent work has shown that deep neural networks exhibit an implicit low-rank simplicity bias. In this paper, we investigate the questions that naturally arise from this observation. What are the temporal consequences of low-rank simplicity bias during optimization? How does representation geometry evolve throughout optimization rather than only at convergence? Do different neural architectures exhibit distinct geometric optimization behaviors? To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale empirical study tracking representational geometry throughout training. We find that neural networks follow three recurring geometric trajectories: persistent high-rank, collapse-and-recovery, and persistent low-rank. We further identify Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC) as a pathological regime in which representations collapse to rank-one and fail to recover, leading to a sustained loss of representational capacity. While collapse-and-recovery is consistently associated with successful optimization in controlled settings, experiments on real-world models show that the relationship between geometric trajectories and optimization outcomes is configuration dependent. Overall, our findings suggest that representation geometry evolves dynamically during training and provide a new perspective on how deep neural networks learn.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) learn task-relevant representations through nonlinear transformations that evolve throughout optimization ( Bengio et al., 2013 ; Saxe et al., 2014 ; Baratin et al., 2021 ) . This evolution, termed representation dynamics , offers insight into how networks learn beyond their final representations. Prior work shows that DNNs exhibit an implicit low-rank bias ( Huh et al., 2023 ) , and that under suitable conditions, finite-depth networks can recover the target function’s rank ( Jacot, 2023 ) . However, existing studies largely characterize representations at convergence, leaving their evolution during optimization less understood. We therefore ask: How does representation geometry evolve during optimization, do architectures exhibit distinct trajectories, and are these trajectories associated with optimization success or failure? Contributions. We investigate these questions and make the following observations. In controlled settings, runs can be partitioned into recurring geometric trajectory archetypes. These trajectories include persistent high-rank behavior, transient representation collapse followed by recovery, and persistent low-rank behavior. The prevalence of these trajectories varies considerably across different architectures, optimization settings, and activation functions. To characterize the pathological extreme of persistent low-rank behavior, we introduce Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC): a persistent rank-one state that, in our experiments, is already present at the first logged epoch and is not escaped during training. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. 1. A large-scale empirical study of temporal representation geometry during optimization.

2. Identification and characterization of three recurring rank trajectories. 3. Introduction of DRC, with evidence that it is present early, grows with depth, and is rarer with residual connections. 4. Statistical evidence that trajectory types are associated with optimization outcomes at convergence. 5. Evidence that trajectory category at early training milestones forecasts eventual optimization success, replicated across synthetic MLPs. 6. CIFAR-10 experiments across MLP, CNN, ResNet, and ViT architectures, replicating the synthetic taxonomy across four architecture families.

Existing work links DNN implicit bias to low-rank representations, neural collapse, and structured feature geometry, but largely studies final representations or optimization behavior rather than temporal evolution of representation. We address this gap through a layer-wise study of 4,084 4{,}084 controlled synthetic runs, identifying trajectory archetypes missed by endpoint analyses. Representation collapse has also been studied in self-supervised learning ( Jing et al., 2022 ) , GNN over-smoothing ( Li et al., 2018 ; Oono and Suzuki, 2020 ) , and Transformer attention collapse ( Dong et al., 2021 ) . Unlike these settings, we study DRC as a persistent rank bottleneck during supervised training associated with optimization failure. Rank contraction in supervised networks has likewise been linked to depth: Daneshmand et al. (2020) found stable-rank collapse at initialization in unnormalized networks, prevented by batch normalization, while Feng et al. (2022) observed decreasing feature and Jacobian rank across layers. Signal-propagation analyses ( Poole et al., 2016 ; Schoenholz et al., 2017 ; Pennington et al., 2017 ) describe ordered and chaotic regimes through the evolution of input correlations; our DRC regime is closely related to the ordered phase, appearing from the first logged epoch and becoming more prevalent with depth. Complementarily, we track full training trajectories, distinguishing runs that escape low-rank states from those that exhibit persistent collapse, and relate these trajectories to optimization outcomes across architectures and optimizers. Although effective rank has been used to assess representation quality and downstream performance ( Garrido et al., 2023 ) , we use it as a training-time criterion for identifying collapse.

In the interest of transparency, we disclose that large language models (specifically OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Anthropic Claude along with Research engines such as Perplexity and Gemini Deep search) were utilized during the preparation of this manuscript under strict authorial oversight for the following specified tasks: • Writing Assistance and Editorial Polishing: LLMs were employed to improve grammatical precision, sentence clarity, academic tone, and typographical flow, as well as to assist with formatting complex L a T e X tables and multi-panel figures. • Literature Retrieval and Discovery: LLMs were queried to assist in identifying and indexing relevant prior literature across dimensional collapse, matrix factorization dynamics, neural network initialization theory, and transformer representation scaling. • Coding and Experimental Assistance: LLMs were used to assist with writing, debugging, and refining experimental code, including data processing, model implementation, training pipelines, and analysis scripts. All generated or suggested code was reviewed, modified, and validated by the authors before use.

Scope of Human Verification and Exclusions: Large language models were not used to generate experimental data, simulate run logs, formulate mathematical proofs, or synthesize scientific conclusions. All empirical runs across multi-seed grids, CIFAR-10 experiments, Singular Value Decompositions (SVD), effective rank/stable rank evaluations, and statistical hypothesis tests were executed on local computational hardware and computed directly from empirical logs. All cited publications, historical attributions, mathematical definitions, and empirical interpretations were verified and cross-checked manually by the authors. The authors retain full accountability and responsibility for the entire scientific content, claims, and integrity of this manuscript.

selections.relevance: Directly tests whether training improves compressibility while preserving language-model quality, and exposes a significant quality tradeoff.

selections.summary: PMRC keeps optimizer states in a gradient subspace and adds a residual-gradient correction. Its LLM pretraining comparison reports the lowest training and validation losses among the tested memory-efficient methods.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses the quality and optimizer-state-memory tradeoff in low-rank LLM pretraining.

evidence.quote: PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods.
PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale.

selections.summary: The paper proves that trace-norm-regularized fine-tuning admits global minimizers with rank controlled by a frozen-feature bottleneck, without NTK linearization. Its stationary-point result for factorized LoRA requires a generic perturbation and does not rule out spurious local minima.
selections.relevance: Directly informs LoRA geometry, nuclear-norm regularization, and principled rank selection.

evidence.quote: we prove that the trace-norm-regularized problem has a global minimizer whose rank is controlled by d Φ d_{\\Phi}
This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation.

selections.summary: ReGRA diagnoses ineffective singular components in a rank-16 LoRA update, then uses residual task gradients to initialize a complementary second-stage adapter within a fixed total rank.
selections.relevance: Connects singular-value structure to practical LoRA rank allocation and downstream performance.

evidence.quote: Without retraining, we evaluate rank- k k approximations formed by retaining the top k k singular components. As shown in Figure 1 , we find that k = 3 k=3 yields the best downstream performance, whereas retaining additional components degrades it.
Under the same total-rank budget, ReGRA consistently achieves stronger overall performance across the evaluated benchmarks and even reaches the performance of the double-rank model.

selections.summary: Studies generalization versus memorization with controlled noise, reporting that projection onto top Fisher eigenvectors separates general task performance from noisy-sample memorization.
selections.relevance: Covers the user’s question about the geometry of memorization under corrupted supervision.

evidence.quote: We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization

selections.summary: Idea2Prior combines identity-aware discovery, candidate assessment, bounded document evidence, and joint ranking. Its reported Hit@5 advantage comes from a small historical comparison whose authors identify sampling and contamination limitations.
selections.relevance: Provides concrete design ideas and evaluation cautions for a handwritten research-digest retrieval harness.

evidence.quote: The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence.
The 30 query cases include overlapping targets and a manually assembled distribution; the first ten items in each tier are not a random sample of all scientific literature.

limitations: Code availability and reproducibility were not verified.
The supplied PMRC passages do not establish full-step throughput, and the supplied ReGRA passages do not quantify its extra calibration or training cost.

2610.23571:83620666d03b7ab3f43b29198bc9b.question: What are BMuon's measured post-training channel-pruning results and language-model results versus Muon and other baselines at matched training compute or model quality? What experiments control for accuracy before pruning?

passages.text: Modern Transformer models incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference time, motivating compression for more efficient deployment ( Kwon et al., 2022 ) . Pruning is a natural approach to this problem, but practical gains depend on the sparsity structure: unstructured sparsity often requires specialized kernels or hardware, whereas structured pruning removes entire computational units and translates directly into efficiency gains ( Wen et al., 2016 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Feed-forward modules can account for roughly two thirds of Transformer parameters ( Geva et al., 2021 ) , making their hidden channels a natural target for structured compression. Global pruning ranks channels across layers jointly, allowing different layers to retain different numbers of channels ( Lee et al., 2021 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Post-pruning fine-tuning adds computational cost, especially for large models ( Kwon et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , motivating compressibility to emerge during training so that pruning requires little or no recovery. Figure 1 : Post-training global MLP pruning on ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16. Mean ± \pm std over 3 seeds. See Appendix E.1 .

Muon has demonstrated strong training efficiency across model scales, from small vision and language-model benchmarks to billion-parameter language models ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) . Its matrix update can be viewed as a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball, giving Muon a steepest-descent interpretation in spectral-norm geometry ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) . Prior work has shown that implicit bias can depend on optimization geometry ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . For Muon, recent theory identifies a spectral-norm margin bias in linear and smooth homogeneous models ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) . Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers degrade rapidly under structured MLP pruning, suggesting that Muon’s spectral geometry does not by itself encourage structured compressibility. As shown in Figure 1 , a Muon-trained ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K collapses after only 30 % 30\% global MLP channel pruning, with Top-1 accuracy falling from 75.23 % 75.23\% to 3.17 % 3.17\% . In contrast, our proposed Budget Muon (BMuon) algorithm retains 74.08 % 74.08\% Top-1 accuracy after 70 % 70\% pruning, nearly matching its 74.17 % 74.17\% accuracy before pruning, with no post-pruning recovery. This raises the central question: can Muon’s spectral geometry be modified to encourage structured compressibility?

To address this question, we introduce BMuon, which reweights Muon’s spectral geometry under a single global budget K K shared across all hidden channels of all MLP blocks. For hidden channel j j in block ℓ \ell , BMuon assigns an allocation μ j ℓ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mu_{j}^{\ell}\in[0,1] to the corresponding row of the up-projection matrix and column of the down-projection matrix, with ∑ ℓ , j μ j ℓ = K \sum_{\ell,j}\mu_{j}^{\ell}=K . For a fixed allocation, BMuon introduces a diagonal reweighting inside Muon’s spectral-norm constraint, with the components of the update variable corresponding to channel j j in block ℓ \ell weighted according to its allocation μ j ℓ \mu_{j}^{\ell} . BMuon chooses the allocation globally, intuitively asking where the update budget should be spent to obtain the greatest first-order decrease in the loss.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

2610.17429:2d96e660693362caed4dea769de88.question: For Monarch-Muon, which measured peak-memory, optimizer-state, and optimizer-step comparisons use the same model architecture, parameter count, hardware, and training setup? How do validation loss or perplexity compare with Monarch-AdamW, dense Muon, and dense AdamW at matched compute or tokens?

passages.text: Figure 2 : MoE pretraining at the same token budget. Two-block Monarch–Muon reaches the reported final validation loss of dense AdamW with fewer active and total parameters. Holding the Monarch factorization fixed isolates the effect of the optimizer. We compare AdamW and Muon with two and four blocks, using the same token budget and training schedule within each architecture. Dense AdamW, dense Muon, and GaLore provide reference losses for the dense quality model. The MoE comparison retains the same routing architecture and changes only the selected projections and their optimizer. Monarch–Muon achieves lower final validation loss than Monarch–AdamW in all four structured comparisons (Table 1 ). The two-block MoE reaches the reported loss of dense AdamW with 15% fewer active parameters and 25.4% fewer total parameters (767M versus 1.029B). Figure 2 places this endpoint in the training trajectory. Thus, matrix-aware updates remain useful when the optimizer acts on structured factors rather than dense weights. Increasing the block count further reduces storage, with a higher final loss under both optimizers. Dense Muon gives the lowest loss in each architecture, defining the quality reference for this representation tradeoff. The learned spectra provide a complementary view of the optimizer effect. At the same block count, Monarch–Muon retains a heavier singular-value tail than Monarch–AdamW in the gate and up projections (Figure 3 ). Similar patterns appear in additional layers and components (Appendix B ). Thus, the change in update geometry reaches the represented matrices, even though orthogonalization is local to their factors.

Figure 3 : Learned gate and up projections in layer 0 of the dense quality model. At the same block count, Muon retains larger singular values in the tail than AdamW. Additional layers and components are in Appendix B .

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. Full-step measurements capture this crossover, which optimizer-step timings alone would miss. Table 2 : Training costs on one H100 at microbatch 4, indexed by the dense reference model size.
