Low precision reduces the bytes and arithmetic cost of the representation that Monarch has already compressed. Following the FP8 approach of COAT ( Xi et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate two separate extensions of the two-block dense quality model: FP8 factor GEMMs with compressed activations, and FP8 optimizer buffers with BF16 GEMMs. Both use the same 39,250-step training recipe, with final loss evaluated in BF16 (Appendix A.5 ). The FP8 computation and activation recipe preserves the optimizer ordering while reducing peak memory by about 31% and training-step time by 14% for Monarch–Muon. Final loss remains within 0.23% of BF16 for both optimizers (Table 5 ). Quantizing optimizer buffers separately gives nearly unchanged loss and reduces their storage by 3.7 × 3.7\times . These results show two complementary uses of low precision: reducing the larger activation footprint and further compressing the already smaller optimizer state. Our implementation quantizes the shared input once and processes the blocks of each factor in one batched FP8 GEMM. Across the large MLP shapes in Table 6 , this gives 1.23 1.23 – 1.46 × 1.46\times faster forward and backward passes than BF16 at the same block count. Standard Transformer Engine FP8 recipes do not consistently accelerate these shapes. At the largest shape, the four-block FP8 MLP is 2.22 × 2.22\times faster than the dense BF16 reference. The layer measurements identify batched execution as a practical complement to the savings of the factorization.

passages.text: Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

2610.22794:de8499f26fefdc0c5cc616bcb9ac1.question: For 1B LLaMA pretraining at matched model size and token budget, what validation loss or perplexity, peak GPU memory, optimizer-state memory, and full-step throughput does Ori report versus GaLore, other low-rank optimizers, and full-rank AdamW? How is the claimed 69.3% performance-gap reduction calculated?

passages.text: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

We thus introduce Ori , a streaming k k -PCA-based O ja-style updated low- r ank i terative optimizer, designed to exploit the slow-drift regime of LLM gradient subspaces. Rather than treating each subspace estimation as an independent, “cold-start” problem—as is the case with periodic SVD recomputation in GaLore—Ori treats subspace estimation as a continuous tracking problem. The core innovation of Ori lies in its drift-aware bootstrapping mechanism: we carry over (transfer) the subspace basis from previous steps as the initialization state for the current step. Because of the slow-drift phenomenon, the prior basis provides a suitable starting point that requires only a few lightweight, streaming k k -PCA-inspired updates to realign with the instantaneous gradient geometry. In practice, Ori instantiates this via the Oja++ algorithm [ 24 , 1 ] , which enables high-frequency basis rotations at a per-step cost of only 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ k 2 ) \mathcal{O}(dk^{2}) . This approach allows for a warm-start transfer of Adam-style first and second moments between successive bases, ensuring stable optimization dynamics. Beyond computational efficiency, we show that this formulation allows Ori to achieve provable sublinear dynamic regret bounds under drift, providing new theoretical tools and guarantees for tracking fidelity that static recomputation methods lack.

Empirically, Ori narrowly tracks the evolving gradient subspace and converts this tracking fidelity into end-to-end wins where it matters most: very low ranks. Under tight rank budgets, each dimension in the projector is precious, and stale misalignment is especially costly. Empirical results show that Ori reduces the performance gap of state-of-the-art low-rank baselines to the full-rank Adam optimizer by up to 69.3% on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task, where the optimizer state rank is 128 in contrast to the model embedding dimension of 2048. And on Roberta-Base fine-tuning tasks, where the ranks are even lower (8 or 4), Ori achieves superior performance on 10 out of 16 scenarios. Moreover, Ori achieved this superior performance with one of the lowest computation budgets. See Figure 1 for a performance–memory overview on LLaMA-1B pre-training, where Ori consistently sits on the bottom-left frontier. Through ablation, we observe that (i) increasing the projector-update period degrades performance—quantifying the cost of staleness, and (ii) injecting a small carry-over (via a drift coefficient ρ ≈ 0.99 \rho\approx 0.99 ) improves accuracy—confirming the value of continuity and statistic transfer. Across pre-training and fine-tuning settings, Ori consistently improves the performance–memory trade-off over LoRA, GaLore, and OSD in the low-rank regime, thereby reducing the gap to full-rank Adam. Our primary contributions in this work are as follows: • We identify and quantify slow gradient subspace drift during LLM training and argue that exploiting its continuity – not merely reacting to it – matters for low-rank optimization.

• We propose Ori, a drift-aware low-rank optimizer that equips gap-free streaming k k -PCA with moment transfer to achieve continuous, high-frequency projector updates at negligible cost. • We provide theoretical support via new dynamic-regret bounds under drift, yielding sublinear regret in the noiseless setting with mild dependence on the consecutive drift parameter. • We present empirical results showing Ori’s superior performance under stringent rank constraints, with ablations isolating the roles of update frequency and drift-aware continuity.

We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

Our answer starts with a simple observation: once the backbone is frozen, the loss does not observe an adapted matrix T T directly, but only through a finite-rank linear map determined by the frozen activations. Concretely, if H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}] is the matrix of frozen input features across the N N training samples, the empirical loss depends on T T only through the product T ​ H TH . We call rank ⁡ ( Φ ) \rank(\Phi) , where Φ ⁡ ( T ) = T ​ H \Phi(T)=TH , the bottleneck rank of the adapted block. The same principle applies blockwise to multiple adapted stages and attention heads. passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA .

This raises a question: how much gradient information lies outside the current tangent space? We analyze the tangent-space residual gradient across ten representative LoRA variants ( Fig. 1 ) and identify two consistent properties. First, the residual accounts for more than 85% of the total gradient energy across all methods. Second, it exhibits strong spectral concentration: the leading singular component captures more than 87% of the residual energy, while the top four capture more than 94%. These findings reveal that the current tangent space leaves substantial gradient information unexploited, yet most of this information can be recovered through a very low-rank approximation. A natural idea to exploit the residual gradient is to continually incorporate its principal directions into the trainable subspace. However, increasing the rank incurs a proportional parameter cost, whereas replacing existing factors at a fixed rank can discard accumulated adaptation information and disrupt training continuity. ReLoRA [ 20 ] , Flora [ 8 ] , and GaLore [ 47 ] also switch low-rank subspaces during training, primarily to overcome rank limitations or reduce training memory, but do not explicitly target gradient components outside the current tangent space. The key challenge is therefore to incorporate these principal residual directions within a fixed rank budget while retaining learned information, maintaining training stability, and preserving mergeability into the pre-trained weights.

To address this challenge, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch that accumulates task-specific directions as in standard LoRA and a dynamic branch that periodically absorbs principal residual directions outside the current tangent space. We prove that, under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints, the optimal update for a local quadratic model is given by the truncated SVD of the tangent-space residual gradient. Crucially, this residual inherits a factored structure from backpropagation, enabling its products with narrow matrices to be computed directly from cached input activations and output gradients. This structure allows us to construct matrix-free operators for Matrix-Free Randomized SVD, which extracts the principal residual directions via randomized SVD [ 7 ] without explicitly forming the residual gradient. To incorporate these directions while maintaining training stability, we introduce Controlled Write-back mechanism, which merges them with the current dynamic branch update, compresses the result back to the original rank, and bounds the relative change at each refresh. After training, both branches are merged into the pre-trained weights, yielding the same inference cost as standard LoRA.

We evaluate DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks: the 19 image classification tasks in VTAB-1K; object detection and instance segmentation on MS COCO; open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation (OVDG-SS) in both real-to-real and synthetic-to-real settings; eight commonsense reasoning tasks using LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B; and GLUE using DeBERTaV3-base. Under matched trainable parameter budgets, DT-LoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and its variants. On MS COCO, DT-LoRA at r = 16 r=16 achieves an average score of 46.6, exceeding LoRA at the same rank by 8.2 points and outperforming LieRA [ 29 ] , which uses twice as many trainable parameters. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA establishes new state-of-the-art results, surpassing the task-specific S 2 -Corr [ 46 ] despite being a general-purpose fine-tuning method. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify a geometric limitation of factorized LoRA: substantial gradient energy lies outside the current tangent space. Across ten representative LoRA variants, we show that this tangent-space residual exhibits strong spectral concentration, and establish that its truncated SVD yields the optimal update under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints for a local quadratic model. • We propose DT-LoRA, which partitions a fixed rank budget into Stable and Dynamic branches to incorporate principal residual directions. Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts these directions without materializing the residual gradient, while Controlled Write-back integrates them with accumulated updates and bounds the change at each refresh, enabling dynamic tangent-space adaptation without additional trainable parameters or inference overhead.

• We demonstrate the effectiveness of DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks, with consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants under matched trainable parameter budgets. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific methods and establishes new state-of-the-art results.

Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts these directions without materializing the residual gradient, while Controlled Write-back integrates them with accumulated updates and bounds the change at each refresh, enabling dynamic tangent-space adaptation without additional trainable parameters or inference overhead.

• We demonstrate the effectiveness of DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks, with consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants under matched trainable parameter budgets. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific methods and establishes new state-of-the-art results.

2610.19700:d7d762d42c1722fe9701b8ee6c575.question: On language-model fine-tuning tasks, what results does ReGRA achieve versus standard LoRA and other rank-allocation methods at the same total rank and training budget? What extra calibration, memory, and training-time costs does its second stage require?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA .

To this end, we train a LoRA model with rank r = 16 r=16 for diagnosis and decompose each learned update Δ ​ 𝑾 \Delta{\bm{W}} using singular value decomposition (SVD). Without retraining, we evaluate rank- k k approximations formed by retaining the top k k singular components. As shown in Figure 1 , we find that k = 3 k=3 yields the best downstream performance, whereas retaining additional components degrades it. This suggests that the full learned update is less effective than a lower-rank approximation of itself. A larger rank budget does not necessarily produce a more useful task-specific update. Figure 1: Effect of retained rank on accuracy. Model performance does not improve monotonically with increasing retained rank.

Motivated by this observation, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation ( ReGRA ), which helps the learned LoRA update make more effective use of its available rank. ReGRA first trains a standard LoRA adapter and then estimates task gradients with a small subset of the training data. To exhaust the allocated rank, we initialize a second-stage adapter with task gradients projected onto the two-sided complement of the first-stage update. With this first-stage estimation, we are able to leave the previously learned components unchanged, yet continually fulfil the update within the allocated rank. During second-stage training, we apply orthogonal regularization to maintain decorrelation between the two stages. After training, both updates can be merged into the base model, introducing no additional inference cost. We evaluate ReGRA using standard LoRA evaluation following ( Hu et al., 2023 ) and expand it to natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Under the same total-rank budget, ReGRA consistently achieves stronger overall performance across the evaluated benchmarks and even reaches the performance of the double-rank model. Ablation studies and further analysis support the effectiveness of residual-gradient initialization and update decorrelation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We reveal that standard LoRA training does not always make effective use of its allocated rank. We approach this problem from a task-gradient perspective, targeting directions not captured by the initial update.

• We propose ReGRA to exhaust the allocated rank. ReGRA is a two-stage adaptation method that estimates task gradients after standard LoRA training, projects out the components captured by the first-stage update, and uses the residual gradients to initialize a second-stage adapter. An orthogonal regularization maintains the decorrelation between the two updates. • We evaluate ReGRA on diverse benchmark sets, showing that it outperforms representative baselines and, in some settings, matches the performance of a model with twice the rank. Ablation studies support the efficacy and rationale of our design.

Low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) represents task-specific weight updates using two trainable low-rank factors, reducing the number of trainable parameters while retaining mergeability at inference ( Hu et al., 2021 ) . Subsequent variants improve its memory and parameter efficiency through quantization, factor freezing, or shared random projections ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ; Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) . Other methods explore adaptive rank allocation and rank-dependent scaling ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Valipour et al., 2023 ; Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) . LoRA+, DoRA, and LoRA-Pro instead improve the optimization or parameterization of low-rank updates ( Hayou et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Recent works also explore adaptive adapter selection and placement to determine where low-rank adaptation is most effective ( Hayou et al., 2026 ; Veprikov et al., 2026 ) . Although these methods improve LoRA from different perspectives, they do not explicitly investigate redundancy among rank components within a learned update matrix.

Spectral and gradient-informed initialization. Several methods initialize LoRA using information from pretrained weights, activations, or downstream data. PiSSA initializes adapters from the principal singular components of pretrained weights, whereas MiLoRA adapts their minor singular components ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . CorDA constructs context-aware adaptation subspaces from weight and activation statistics, while EVA selects initialization directions according to activation variance ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Paischer et al., 2026 ) . Gradient-based methods use the task gradient at the start of fine-tuning to guide adapter initialization ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Ponkshe et al., 2024 ) . These approaches determine the adaptation subspace before fine-tuning, whereas ReGRA estimates residual task gradients after a first-stage update has been learned.

passages.text: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW’s previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output’s estimated spectral norm sets each matrix’s threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline’s final smoothed training loss in 7.2% fewer steps.

The first 40 successful optimizer updates use global clipping at norm 1 to initialize moments and histories. A selected matrix enters the spectral branch when its previous second moment, history, and participation count are ready. Other tensors use a threshold λ ​ f \lambda f , where f f tracks their clipped output norms. These tensors include the MoE experts and embeddings, so the output-norm controller covers a large part of the model. Appendix B specifies initialization, intermittent participation, and checkpoint restoration. The distributed implementation all-gathers gradient fragments into complete logical matrices, applies the transformation, and writes each rank’s local optimizer slice. Stored row and column summaries recover the previous second-moment scale without repeatedly gathering the full moment tensor. The transform uses FP32 within BF16 training ( Micikevicius et al., 2018 ) . 2610.20857:79b7cd051db0ff5db5f40023d2413.question: How is IDEA2PRIOR evaluated for paper retrieval and ranking? What are the baselines, query counts, relevance judgments, retrieval corpus controls, and limitations of the reported Hit@5 comparison? Which components could inform an application-controlled research-digest harness?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

The 30 query cases include overlapping targets and a manually assembled distribution; the first ten items in each tier are not a random sample of all scientific literature. Benchmark authoring used an LLM, browser build identifiers were unavailable, history contamination cannot be excluded retrospectively, and one baseline credit follows an explicit historical convention. These factors limit causal and statistical interpretation. Future evaluation should freeze inputs, use isolated sessions, report first-attempt and recovered performance separately, and obtain independent relevance judgments for every returned work.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

The 30 query cases include overlapping targets and a manually assembled distribution; the first ten items in each tier are not a random sample of all scientific literature. Benchmark authoring used an LLM, browser build identifiers were unavailable, history contamination cannot be excluded retrospectively, and one baseline credit follows an explicit historical convention. These factors limit causal and statistical interpretation. Future evaluation should freeze inputs, use isolated sessions, report first-attempt and recovered performance separately, and obtain independent relevance judgments for every returned work.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) learn task-relevant representations through nonlinear transformations that evolve throughout optimization ( Bengio et al., 2013 ; Saxe et al., 2014 ; Baratin et al., 2021 ) . This evolution, termed representation dynamics , offers insight into how networks learn beyond their final representations. Prior work shows that DNNs exhibit an implicit low-rank bias ( Huh et al., 2023 ) , and that under suitable conditions, finite-depth networks can recover the target function’s rank ( Jacot, 2023 ) . However, existing studies largely characterize representations at convergence, leaving their evolution during optimization less understood. We therefore ask: How does representation geometry evolve during optimization, do architectures exhibit distinct trajectories, and are these trajectories associated with optimization success or failure? Contributions. We investigate these questions and make the following observations. In controlled settings, runs can be partitioned into recurring geometric trajectory archetypes. These trajectories include persistent high-rank behavior, transient representation collapse followed by recovery, and persistent low-rank behavior. The prevalence of these trajectories varies considerably across different architectures, optimization settings, and activation functions. To characterize the pathological extreme of persistent low-rank behavior, we introduce Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC): a persistent rank-one state that, in our experiments, is already present at the first logged epoch and is not escaped during training. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. 1. A large-scale empirical study of temporal representation geometry during optimization.

2. Identification and characterization of three recurring rank trajectories. 3. Introduction of DRC, with evidence that it is present early, grows with depth, and is rarer with residual connections. 4. Statistical evidence that trajectory types are associated with optimization outcomes at convergence. 5. Evidence that trajectory category at early training milestones forecasts eventual optimization success, replicated across synthetic MLPs. 6. CIFAR-10 experiments across MLP, CNN, ResNet, and ViT architectures, replicating the synthetic taxonomy across four architecture families.

Existing work links DNN implicit bias to low-rank representations, neural collapse, and structured feature geometry, but largely studies final representations or optimization behavior rather than temporal evolution of representation. We address this gap through a layer-wise study of 4,084 4{,}084 controlled synthetic runs, identifying trajectory archetypes missed by endpoint analyses. Representation collapse has also been studied in self-supervised learning ( Jing et al., 2022 ) , GNN over-smoothing ( Li et al., 2018 ; Oono and Suzuki, 2020 ) , and Transformer attention collapse ( Dong et al., 2021 ) . Unlike these settings, we study DRC as a persistent rank bottleneck during supervised training associated with optimization failure. Rank contraction in supervised networks has likewise been linked to depth: Daneshmand et al. (2020) found stable-rank collapse at initialization in unnormalized networks, prevented by batch normalization, while Feng et al. (2022) observed decreasing feature and Jacobian rank across layers. Signal-propagation analyses ( Poole et al., 2016 ; Schoenholz et al., 2017 ; Pennington et al., 2017 ) describe ordered and chaotic regimes through the evolution of input correlations; our DRC regime is closely related to the ordered phase, appearing from the first logged epoch and becoming more prevalent with depth. Complementarily, we track full training trajectories, distinguishing runs that escape low-rank states from those that exhibit persistent collapse, and relate these trajectories to optimization outcomes across architectures and optimizers. Although effective rank has been used to assess representation quality and downstream performance ( Garrido et al., 2023 ) , we use it as a training-time criterion for identifying collapse.

selections.summary: BMuon changes Muon’s spectral geometry to encourage structured MLP-channel pruning. In a 1B LLaMA-style model, it preserved its unpruned perplexity through 80% pruning, but had worse unpruned perplexity than Muon (12.84 versus 10.92).
selections.relevance: Direct test of whether training can improve compressibility without sacrificing quality; the observed quality tradeoff is important.

evidence.quote: On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning.
BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking.

selections.summary: Monarch-Muon applies matrix-aware updates to structured factors. At a 6.89B dense reference size, reported peak memory falls from 68.87 to 52.94 GB versus dense Muon; fixed-structure comparisons favor Monarch-Muon over Monarch-AdamW on validation loss.
selections.relevance: Combines factorization, Muon, learned spectra, and measured quality–memory–speed tradeoffs across model sizes.

evidence.quote: Monarch–Muon achieves lower final validation loss than Monarch–AdamW in all four structured comparisons (Table 1 ).

selections.summary: PMRC adds orthogonal residual-gradient correction to subspace optimization. In LLM pretraining comparisons through 1.3B parameters, the paper reports the lowest training and validation losses among its memory-efficient baselines.

evidence.quote: We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) .
PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods.

selections.summary: Provides a non-NTK account of low-rank LoRA solutions: trace-norm regularization selects a low-rank update governed by a finite-rank observation bottleneck. Its stationary-point result requires a generic positive-semidefinite perturbation and does not exclude spurious local minima.
selections.relevance: Directly informs LoRA geometry, nuclear-norm regularization, and rank selection.

evidence.quote: Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output.
This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation.

selections.summary: DT-LoRA uses a stable and a dynamic branch within a fixed rank budget to capture leading residual-gradient directions outside LoRA’s current tangent space. The paper reports improvements over LoRA variants under matched trainable-parameter budgets.
selections.relevance: Directly studies spectral concentration and optimization geometry in practical low-rank fine-tuning.

candidates.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to c
candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW's previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: T-MUON: Tensorizing Muon via t-SVD for Large Language Model Pre-training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has recently emerged as a strong optimizer for large language model pretraining by exploiting matrix structure through polar orthogonalization. However, it processes each parameter matrix independently, whereas recent tensor-aware extensions of Muon jointly update groups of eligible matrix parameters through matrix unfoldings. In contrast, we propose T-MUON, a t-SVD-based generalization that groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors and defines the corresponding Muon-style update directly through the $M$-transform. candidates.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. candidates.title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. candidates.title: The Ephemeral Cost of Switching Optimizers Across LLM Training Stages
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. candidates.title: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights.

While orthogonalized update rules, such as the recently introduced Muon optimizer, have shown strong empirical performance and scalability, their behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) is not yet understood. In this paper, we propose DP-Muon, a differentially private variant of the Muon optimizer. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Recent work has shown that deep neural networks exhibit an implicit low-rank simplicity bias. In this paper, we investigate the questions that naturally arise from this observation. What are the temporal consequences of low-rank simplicity bias during optimization? candidates.abstract_excerpt: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. candidates.title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. candidates.abstract_excerpt: The training loss of binary and ternary neural networks, expanded as a multilinear polynomial over the discrete weights, is structurally equivalent to the energy of a hierarchical high-order Ising model. We exploit this equivalence to apply Ising solvers to discrete-weight network training, while accounting for a fundamental difference in objectives: an Ising solver seeks the ground state of a fixed energy function, whereas training seeks solutions that generalize to unseen data. candidates.title: Sparse Federated Echo State Networks for Time-Series Classification via Smooth-L1 Regularization
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Echo State Networks (ESNs), as lightweight implementations of reservoir computing, provide efficient solutions for temporal data processing in resource-constrained environments. While standard ESNs offer computational efficiency, their dense readout layers inflate the stored model and the per-sample inference cost. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Releasing a neural network checkpoint can leak information about its training data, and existing reconstruction results rely on gradient-descent training. We ask whether the choice of optimizer affects the ability to recover the training data. Extending work connecting Karush--Kuhn--Tucker conditions to training-data reconstruction, we show that the implicit biases of popular optimizers (SGD, Adam, Muon) leave very different fingerprints of the training data. candidates.title: Scalable Levenberg-Marquardt Training Framework for Deep Learning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: The Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithm is a widely used nonlinear least-squares solver known for its rapid convergence. For small-scale neural networks, LMA provides better convergence and architectural robustness than first-order optimizers like Adam. However, LMA imposes prohibitive memory and computational costs. These costs are primarily from the Jacobian matrix, whose dimensions scale with both the number of samples and parameters. This bottleneck prevents its use in large-scale neural networks. candidates.title: Making LoRA Identifiable: Orthogonal Alignment for Continual Learning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: There is growing interest in applying Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) to Continual Learning, as it enables faster training, mitigates catastrophic forgetting, and facilitates better adaptation to new tasks. Prior approaches have explored a range of strategies, including extending new LoRA branches for each incoming task, training under orthogonal loss objectives across all task-specific LoRA modules, and employing gating mechanisms to integrate new and existing LoRA modules. candidates.title: Bridging Compressed Communication and Local Steps via Spectral Method in Federated Learning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of complex models across large-scale networks of edge devices while keeping data localized. However, data heterogeneity and high communication overhead remain fundamental bottlenecks. Recently, the spectral optimizer Muon has demonstrated remarkable advantages over Adam-like methods in centralized training. candidates.title: Memory-Efficient Integer-Only Training of Deep Neural Networks
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training neural networks in reduced precision can yield significant efficiency gains, yet all existing methods that scale to standard computer vision benchmarks retain floating-point in at least one stage, typically the weight update or optimizer state. We present a training algorithm that scales to modern deep neural networks, in which every tensor (weights, gradients, and activations) is stored as INT8, and every operation (forward pass, backward pass, weight update, optimizer update) is performed in integer arithmetic. candidates.title: Mixed Precision Scaling Laws for Quantized Pretraining
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Since scaling laws were introduced for modern LLMs (Kaplan et al., 2020), several works have extended them to account for quantization, tracking the emerging low-precision data types supported on AI accelerators. candidates.title: From Parallel to Sequential: Small-Batch Noise Restores Simplicity Bias of Muon
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Simplicity bias, which can arise from sequential feature learning during training, has been proposed as a general explanation for the success of deep learning. An important driver of this phenomenon is saddle-to-saddle behavior, in which the gradient flow trajectory remains close to a sequence of saddle manifolds while learning one feature at a time. candidates.title: FedLoRD: Personalized Federated Learning based on Low-Rank Structures of Model Parameter Differences

PFL is a branch of federated learning that aims to learn models tailored to the local data of each client under biased local data distributions.
